title: Why you CHEATING!? | Ruy Lopez | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The pawn to e4, e5.
The knight to f3.
The most basic openings are the ones where you copy your opponent's move — e4 and e5, or d4 and d5.
The knight to f3 — of course we play the knight to c6.
The knight to c6.

The bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, also known as the Spanish, the most popular opening at the highest levels, around for over 500 years and named after a priest who extolled it in the 1500s. White develops a piece to do something — here the bishop pressures the knight, and since the knight defends the pawn, indirectly White pressures the pawn.
We follow the main line with a6, chasing the bishop away from b5. White must decide: take on c6 — the Exchange Variation — or drop the bishop back to a4.
The bishop takes c6 — a legitimate move. Aren't we blundering a pawn if White then grabs e5? It's actually a trap a lot of beginners miss. Which pawn do we recapture with?
The queen to d4 — to enable that, we have to recapture with the d-pawn. There's a rule to take toward the centre, but it's highly overrated; always weigh the pros and cons.
Taking toward the centre would be the b-pawn, but a move that follows the rules isn't necessarily good —
— the d-pawn recapture opens the bishop for quicker development and, more importantly, takes the sting out of the knight takes e5, because we bring our queen up to d4.

He knows not to take the pawn, and he castles. Now we have to do something about the e5-pawn, which is hanging — the knight takes e5 is a threat. Many ways to defend it: directly with f6 or the bishop to d6, or indirectly with the bishop to g4, pinning the knight. I'll play the old main line —
— f6, historically considered the most solid response to the Exchange Variation, even though it violates the basic rules of development.
d4. It makes Ben Finegold cringe, and where is the knight going to go —
— do we just not care about developing our knight?

That's why I'm playing this — to explain a couple of specific properties that make f6 not only possible but quite effective. d4 is correct, and it's an important moment: if we take on d4 we play into White's hands, opening the centre. Having played f6 we've physically weakened our king, and we've developed nothing — the one piece we developed was exchanged — so it's important to keep the centre closed, or better, trade queens, since trading queens makes it less likely your opponent checkmates you.
So the best move, the one I just mentioned, is the bishop to g4 — pinning the knight, since behind it stands the more valuable queen, so the knight can't move.
c3 — also a good move, reinforcing the d4-pawn.
Had White taken on e5, we'd have traded queens and recaptured — I'll talk about that endgame after the game.
c3 reinforces the d4-pawn. Now we develop our pieces — nothing extraordinary, but there's a really cool move I remember analyzing —
— most people play the bishop to d6, and that's what we play too, for solid, simple chess, though it's not the move I actually play over the board; I'll show that after.
The knight to d2 — our opponent continues developing well, and we should keep developing too.
We need to develop the knight from g8, our last piece preventing castling. The knight to h6 is awkward — you don't usually develop knights to the rim — so the knight to e7.
h3 — he's playing all the top theoretical moves. As a beginner there's a temptation to trade the knight on f3, but —
— there's no need: the bishop was pinning White's knight to the queen, a valuable bishop, so we simply drop it back to h5, preserving the pin. Retreating moves are never inherently bad.
It's perfectly acceptable. As a beginner you might fear g4 chasing that bishop away —
— but g4 pushes a pawn in front of your own king, and when you push pawns in front of your own king, it becomes more exposed —
— and those pawns become easier to attack; g4 would play right into our hands.
The pawns come off; we simply recapture with the f-pawn, and I think the queen to b3 is the theoretical move.
The knight to c4 — I already don't know the theory here, but it's also very good.

Let's figure out this position. There's no problem — we just castle, and we're not blundering our bishop, because the c7-pawn guards the bishop on d6. By castling we exert more pressure on the knight on f3, still pinning it. But the queen to b3 is a very powerful move: it sets up an x-ray against our king and unpins the knight, which can now move without fear of losing White's queen. Our top priority is to deal with that x-ray, which in many cases leads to a discovered check — White threatens the knight takes d6 with a devastating check.
